interface.name: gyro_scene_v1

description.summary: where the windows are, said by the shell

interface.description:
A shell arranges the windows of its session: it groups them into containers, decides where each one goes, and says what kind of change every batch of that is. The compositor owns what the change looks like.
That division is the whole of this protocol. A shell may invent any arrangement - a grid, a ring, a stack of cards, a fisheye dock - and it may not invent a motion. What a person gets from that is two desktops built on this compositor that look nothing alike and feel like the same machine, because everything on both of them accelerates, overshoots and settles identically. A shell that could write its own springs would be a shell whose overview animates a little differently from the launcher beside it, and nobody would be able to say why the machine felt cheap.
So there is no request here that carries a duration, a curve, a damping ratio or a frame. What a shell says is a destination and a name for the kind of change, and the compositor decides how the world gets there.
Everything a shell says is double-buffered and applied by commit, and a commit carries the timestamp of the input event behind it. That timestamp is the point of it rather than a detail: two clients answering the same keystroke name the same instant, so the compositor composes their separate commits into one gesture, and a commit that arrives a frame late renders already in progress by exactly the right amount instead of starting late.
Every object here belongs to a client the compositor has granted the run of a session, and an application is never offered this global. A client able to move other people's windows is a client able to hide the one somebody is typing into.

request.name: destroy
request.description:
Destroys the object, releasing placement if this client had claimed it - so the compositor goes back to placing windows itself, exactly as it does while no shell is running.
Containers are not affected and do not go away. They belong to the compositor, and outliving the shell that asked for them is what they are for: see get_container.
Anything staged and not yet committed is discarded.

request.name: claim_placement
request.description:
Says that this client decides where a new window of this session goes. Until it does, the compositor places windows itself, centred on the screen holding the pointer.
A window is invisible until it is placed, so this is not a preference the compositor can be wrong about while the shell catches up: a shell that claims placement and then never places anything gets a session where nothing appears. That is deliberate, and the alternative is worse - a window shown where the compositor guessed and then jumped to where the shell wanted it, on every window a person ever opens.
A shell that has claimed placement is told about new windows through ext_foreign_toplevel_list_v1, the same way it learns about every other window, and answers with place_window.
Only one client may hold this at a time, and a second claim is the placement_taken error. Unlike a claimed chord, which several clients may hold at once because a keystroke can be told to all of them, placement has exactly one answer - two placers would be a window put in two places in one frame. Failing loudly is the point: a shell that silently did not place would look to a person like a compositor that had stopped opening windows.
Placement is released when this object is destroyed or the client goes away, which is what lets the compositor keep a session usable across a shell restart.

request.name: get_container
request.description:
Creates a container - a node with a position and a visibility of its own, which windows can be put into and which moves everything in it when it moves. A workspace, an overview grid, a stack.
The name is the shell's to mint, and it is what makes the container survive the shell. Containers belong to the compositor, not to the client that asked for one: a shell that crashes and respawns calls this again with the same names and gets the same containers back, with the same windows still in them and still where they were. What that spares a person is re-sorting forty windows after a crash they did not cause.
So this creates or re-adopts, and the state event says which happened by reporting the position and visibility the container actually has. For a new container that is what was asked for here. For one that was already there it is what survived, and the arguments to this request are ignored.
The position is where the container sits, and it is applied immediately rather than at the next commit - a container being born has nowhere to move from, so there is nothing for a transition to describe. This is the only place in this protocol where a shell states a position that does not animate, and it is the reason commit has no way to ask for no animation.
Containers are created in the session's floor, which is the compositor's own container that everything hangs under. They cannot be nested inside each other yet.
An empty name, or one longer than 256 bytes, is the bad_name error: a container that cannot be named is one that cannot be re-adopted, which defeats the point of having asked for it.

arg.name: name
arg.summary: the shell's own name for it, stable across restarts

arg.name: x
arg.summary: position, if this call creates it

arg.name: y
arg.summary: position, if this call creates it

arg.name: z
arg.summary: position, if this call creates it

request.name: place_window
request.description:
Says where a window goes and what it is in. Double-buffered: it takes effect at the next commit.
A null container puts the window on the session's floor, which is where it already is if nothing has moved it. A shell with no containers at all uses this and nothing else.
The first placement of a window is its entrance. The position lands rather than animating - there is nowhere for a window to travel from before it has been anywhere - and the compositor then plays the window opening at the commit's timestamp. The transition named on that commit is not consulted for this window, because what an arriving window does is the compositor's to decide and getting it wrong is the most visible frame in the system. What the timestamp is for is that the entrance starts when the person pressed the key, not when the shell got round to answering.
Every later placement of the same window is an ordinary move under the commit's transition.
A window whose client has already closed it - a handle that has received ext_foreign_toplevel_handle_v1.closed - is silently ignored rather than being an error. An application quitting while the shell is mid-commit is ordinary, and a shell cannot avoid the race by being careful.

arg.name: container
arg.summary: what to put it in, or null for the session's floor

request.name: commit

description.summary: apply everything staged, as one change

request.description:
Applies everything staged since the last commit, as one change of one named kind, starting at one instant.
Everything in one commit shares that instant, so a workspace sliding out and the window being focused inside it start together whatever order the requests were sent in. Everything in one commit is also seen at once: no frame is ever drawn with half of it applied.
The transition is the name of what kind of change this is, and it is the only thing a shell says about motion. The compositor holds a table of springs per transition per property, so naming one is naming a whole coordinated motion rather than a setting - and a property added to that table later starts animating at every shell that already exists, without any of them being changed.
There is deliberately no way to say "no transition". Every change a shell makes is a change a person is watching, and the state a shell wants to set without motion - where a container sits when it is first made - is stated at get_container instead, before there is anything on screen to move. Left available, a shell could set a position with no animation sixty times a second and hand-animate the desktop itself, which is exactly the cohesion this protocol exists to hold.
The timestamp is the instant the input event behind this change was reported by its device, on CLOCK_MONOTONIC - the same value gyro_binding_v1.pressed carries, and the reason that event carries it. For a change no input event is behind, such as a monitor being plugged in, the shell's own clock reading is correct and honest. A timestamp later than the compositor's own reading of the clock is treated as now, because a change stamped into the future is one that stands still until the clock catches up, which reads as the machine having hung.
A transition this compositor does not know is the bad_transition error. A commit with nothing staged is legal and does nothing.

arg.name: transition
arg.summary: the kind of change this is

arg.name: tv_sec_hi
arg.summary: high 32 bits of the seconds part of the timestamp

arg.name: tv_sec_lo
arg.summary: low 32 bits of the seconds part of the timestamp

enum.name: transition

description.summary: the kinds of change the compositor knows how to draw

enum.description:
A closed set, and it grows by the compositor learning a new kind of change rather than by a client describing one. Each name stands for a coordinated motion across every property it touches, designed as one thing.
There is no entry for "none", and commit says why.

entry.name: focus_change
entry.summary: attention moving from one window to another

entry.name: matched_move
entry.summary: something travelling from where it was to where it now is

entry.name: placement_taken
entry.summary: another client is already placing this session's windows

entry.name: bad_name
entry.summary: the container name is empty or too long

entry.name: bad_transition
entry.summary: the transition is not one this compositor knows

interface.name: gyro_container_v1
interface.description:
A container the compositor holds on this shell's behalf: a position, a visibility, and whatever has been placed inside it. Moving it moves everything in it as one, which is what a workspace switch is.
It is the compositor's rather than the client's, so this object is a reference to it and not the thing itself. Destroying the object leaves the container standing; remove is how a container actually goes away.

request.name: destroy
request.description:
Destroys this object. The container itself is untouched, along with everything in it.
That is the opposite of what destroying an object usually means, and it is the whole reason containers are named. A shell exits or crashes and every object it held is destroyed; if that took the containers with it, a crash would dissolve every workspace in the session and pile forty windows into one heap. Instead the panel blinks out and comes back, and the arrangement it comes back to is the one the person left.
Anything staged on this container and not yet committed is discarded.

request.name: remove
request.description:
Removes the container. Anything still in it returns to the session's floor, at the position it had inside the container, so a window is never left with nowhere to be.
This object stays valid and inert afterwards, and every request on it does nothing; the client should destroy it.
This is the deliberate act, as against destroy above. A person closing a workspace does this; a shell exiting does not.

request.name: set_position
request.description:
Sets where the container sits. Double-buffered: it takes effect at the next gyro_scene_v1.commit, under that commit's transition.
Everything in the container moves with it, as one thing rather than as several - which is what makes a workspace switch a single sliding surface instead of a dozen windows travelling in loose formation.

request.name: set_visible
request.description:
Shows or hides the container and everything under it. Double-buffered: it takes effect at the next gyro_scene_v1.commit.
Hiding is immediate and does not animate, whatever the commit says: there is nothing between shown and hidden to draw. A shell that wants a workspace to fade out moves it or fades it under a transition and hides it afterwards.
A hidden container still holds its windows, still keeps their positions, and still costs the compositor nothing to skip.

event.name: state
event.description:
Sent once, immediately after the container is created or re-adopted, and never again.
For a container this call created, it repeats what was asked for. For one that was already there, it is what survived - which is how a shell that has just restarted learns that its workspaces are where it left them rather than where it would have put them.
What this does not yet carry is what is in the container. A restarted shell knows its containers are back and does not know which window is in which, so it cannot redraw a workspace strip without asking every window where it is. That is missing rather than withheld.
